turns.name: Tim O'Reilly
turns.text:
I want to start with a number. In our study of about 14,000 real search-enabled LLM conversations, citation efficiency varied from 0.19 to 0.45. That's the extra citations a model gives for each additional relevant page it reads, measured on identical queries. So when a system reads ten pages and credits three, that's a design choice. The best systems already show that transparent attribution is feasible today. What's missing is coordination and incentives, and that makes this a mechanism-design problem.

We've solved problems like this before. PageRank, the ad auction and YouTube's Content ID were all engineered rules that got self-interested actors to disclose honestly and send value back. YouTube's line to rights holders was "How about we help you monetize it instead?" At O'Reilly we built Answers on RAG. Because we know which content produced an answer, we cite it and pay authors in proportion to their contribution. If a publisher our size can do that, the labs can too.

So here's what I think a well-designed marketplace needs.

First, telemetry. Standardize two fields, document hashes and relevance scores, so anyone can check what a model consumed and how faithfully it credited it. Ivan convinced me this morning that we need a third element: the source's status has to travel in the trace. A citation to a retracted paper has perfect provenance and is still wrong. Without status, "no payment without provenance" just pays for errors efficiently. Leslie's warning matters too. Complying has to cost the smallest diamond journal nothing, or a cheap standard turns into a toll.

Second, pay for the output, not the training. Lump-sum licensing deals entrench the richest labs, rarely reach the actual creators, and amount to selling the chicken so the licensee gets the eggs. Nick is right that fine-grained splits may not work across all of scholarship. So pay per use at the level of the journal or society, and let those communities govern how it's divided.

Third, fund the exoskeleton. Crossref, OpenAlex, ORCID and Retraction Watch are what gives AI science its credibility, and they run on a shoestring. Right now the relationship is almost entirely extractive. Labs should check citations against them by default, contribute metadata back and pay for them. That isn't philanthropy. It's enlightened self-interest.

Fourth, build protocols, not platforms. A protocol is an engineered argument. An API is an engineered agreement imposed by whoever dominates. Keep it open, federated and inspectable, so no single registry becomes either the monoculture or the policeman.

And make disclosure of search traces a condition of purchase for anyone buying these systems. That's the lever we actually have.

recall.query: attribution gap LLM search pages read versus cited telemetry
pay for the output not the training O'Reilly Answers royalties
collaborative exoskeleton scholarly infrastructure AI labs fund Crossref OpenAlex Retraction Watch
missing mechanisms protocols market-shaping engineered argument

turns.name: Alex Springer
turns.text:
I'm the outsider here. I come from affiliate and commerce tech, not scholarly publishing. But my view of the marketplace is simple: plumbing before prices.

Search pointed you to content, so the value chain was legible. AI digests the content and hands back the value as if it were its own. Three things are missing: identity, measurement and value return. Without measurement, attribution is impossible, and every argument about levies, licences or royalties this week rests on records nobody is keeping.

So the design is a chain. The source declares its terms, through RSL or Creative Commons. The agent proves who it is. Then usage gets recorded as discrete events: retrieved, grounded, cited, presented, engaged. Tim's document hash is our content ID field, and a DOI works fine there.

The core design choice is two witnesses. The agent stamps each fetch with an ID, and the publisher's CDN logs the same ID. Neither side has to trust the other. I want to be honest about the limit, though. Only retrieval has an independent witness on the publisher's side. Grounding and citation need the providers to report, so every licence needs an event-level reporting clause.

Why now? Our May audit covered 24,127 citations. 7.8% came from domains blocking the provider's training bot. Checked against the live-search bot, the figure falls to 2.1%. That gap exists because robots.txt can't tell training apart from grounding. Training is effectively permanent, while grounding is per query and can be revoked. They need separate controls.

Three answers to challenges from this morning. First, on surveillance: we identify the agent, never the reader. The end user isn't a party to the telemetry, and whoever holds the data should publish their retention policies. Second, Geoffrey is right that an identity manifest is an agent asserting things about itself. It only means something once other parties attest to it. Third, Ivan's point: status should travel as an extension field, so a citation to a retracted paper is flagged, not paid.

On cost: retrieval telemetry works today from logs you already have. Our CDN worker is open source and free, the specs are Apache-licensed, and there's no dependency on any operator. Leslie, if complying costs a diamond journal anything, we've failed. And Adrian, fairly asked who pays for us: OpenAttribution is a not-for-profit, and governance should be one member, one vote.

What I won't give you is a pricing formula. Telemetry doesn't decide ownership, price or compensation. That belongs to the communities, Tim's societies included. But I'll hold one line. Whoever takes a margin on the count shouldn't set the count.

recall.query: identity, measurement, value return chain for AI content market
two independent witnesses CDN log agent log Content-Telemetry-ID
telemetry does not determine price or compensation, neutral measurement governance
audit citations from blocked domains bot-taxonomy gap crawl-to-referral ratio

turns.name: Nick Vincent
turns.text:
I'll start with where we actually are. I'd call it a quasi-enclosure. Value still flows back to the public, which is why AI looks like a public good. But what comes back are subsidized club goods: products built by processing the commons, still dependent on our ongoing data labor, and they can have their subsidy cut, be withdrawn, or be redirected whenever their owners choose. Reuse without attribution also starves the places where curation happens, and in the end that hurts AI too. So a well-designed marketplace has to do three things.

First, price attested human judgment, not raw tokens. Tim and Alex have described the retrieval layer, and I agree with almost all of it. I'd push the same logic across the whole supply chain. Data creators attest that their material went into training. Expert reviewers attest that they took part in an evaluation. Outputs carry attestations of which model produced them and what was retrieved, and papers written with AI help carry all of that forward. Ivan's point applies at every link: status has to travel with the record. Provenance isn't validation.

Second, collective bargaining. On its own, a single author can't hold out against a market where the price of information tends to zero. Evaluation data is where scholars have real leverage right now. Good evals are just good data, and labs can't grade frontier models without expert judgment. The default path is centralized gig labor. The alternative is data guilds and trusts growing out of societies, editorial boards and bodies like the ACM. They would bargain over terms, and they would also set standards, rule on quality and keep provenance. This morning Geoff and Henry added the conditions I'd now build in: these bodies must be representative and forkable. And Leslie is right that refusing a deal has to be an outcome someone will fund.

Third, a commons backstop, because I don't think everything should be turned into a market. My proposal is a presumptive commons-rent tax. We presume that some share of AI rents comes from the commons. A firm can bring that share down by documenting licensed or reciprocal provenance, which means paying into Wikipedia, OpenAlex or Crossref counts in its favor. Selena and Katherine showed the model: keep the content free, charge for reliable access, and companies pay anyway. Payouts should go coarsely, to communities and collections, until we can actually trace individual pieces of text. Tim moving to the journal or society level is the same move.

Now Adrian's question: who funds and polices attestation? Public tax authorities set the rules. Accredited auditors review the evidence and are funded from the tax. A public technical board maintains the schemas. Institutional buyers make disclosure a condition of purchase. And following Alex, the counters should never be the ones taking a margin on the count.

recall.query: collective bargaining for information, data guilds, evaluation data leverage
attestation across the AI supply chain, who verifies, auditors
presumptive commons-rent tax, coarse disbursement, reciprocity payments
paradox of reuse quasi-enclosure subsidized club goods

turns.name: James Evans
turns.text:
I support most of this. Nick's guilds and Tim's payments at the society level fit what I've argued: collective management organizations already show how money can reach huge numbers of rights holders without negotiating each deal. The pricing objection is also weaker than people think. Labs already decide how to weight their data mixtures, and scaling laws tell them what extra data is worth.

My worry is the unit being counted. Pay per citation and you pay for what already draws attention. Our Nature data shows AI-assisted work crowding onto popular, data-rich topics under the lamp post. A marketplace that pays on citation counts pays for that same hill-climbing. And the most valuable things models are missing, null results, failed replications and notebooks of dead ends, never show up in a citation trace. After ChatGPT, null claims in abstracts dropped sharply. So some of Nick's commons rent should be set aside to deliberately gather negative knowledge. Nobody will ever cite it, and that's why a market won't pay for it.

recall.query: collective licensing collective management organizations pay rights holders
negative knowledge null results registered reports dead ends training data
AI narrows science citation concentration popular well-lit questions

turns.name: Henry Farrell
turns.text:
I'm broadly with all three talks. My one-line version of the problem has been that models are an obligate complement to human knowledge. Unless enough of the proceeds reach the people who produce it, the system eats its own foundations. Nick's guilds are the SAG-AFTRA lesson applied to scholarship. But the lesson this morning taught me is that blocs run by incumbents turn into enclosure. So representation and forkability aren't extras. They're the whole point. Alex's rule that whoever takes a margin on the count shouldn't set the count is a good piece of political economy.

But James has found the hole. Telemetry only measures what already travels, and these systems are centripetal. They strain out the rare and the novel. Paying on citations pays for that pull. So along with Nick's set-aside for negative results, funders should test whether AI review can even recognize novelty before anyone lets it screen papers. My bet is that it can't.

recall.query: obligate complement paying knowledge producers self-sustaining
homogenization novelty strained out AI peer review
organize countervailing power collective bargaining SAG-AFTRA

turns.name: Tamar Gendler
turns.text:
The Israeli daycare story is the warning I'd put next to all three talks. The centre started fining parents who picked up late, and more parents came late. Once there was a price, lateness looked like something you could buy. Pay scholars per citation and you may do the same to refereeing, sleuthing and sharing null results, which people now do because the community expects it of them. We'd risk turning a norm into a fee schedule. That's how I read James's point. The unpaid, uncited work is exactly what gets pushed out once some of the work is paid.

Nick's idea of pricing attested human judgment points the right way. In my terms, it pays the terminal nodes, the people who actually do first-order evaluation, not the links that pass their verdicts along. But how the money is framed matters as much as the amount. Paying communities, not individual counts, may keep the frame collegial. I don't know that it will. Nobody can derive incentive design from first principles yet, so pilot it and watch what people start doing differently.

recall.query: credentialing paired with learning, incentives crowd out motivation
terminal nodes trust network turtles all the way down
paying people changes what they do, daycare fine, markets and norms

turns.name: Brent Hecht
turns.text:
I agree with all three talks, and I'll say it as someone who works at one of the companies doing the buying. My view is that the old deal between model builders and content producers rested on two things: producers didn't see the value they were creating, and the models weren't competing with them. Both are gone, and scientific papers are part of that supply chain. What Tim, Alex and Nick have laid out is the start of a new grand bargain.

Two points. First, Nick is right that producers have leverage. When models are trained only on data whose owners explicitly consented, they lose a lot of performance. That suggests withholding organized by professional domain would actually bite, and science is one of those domains.

Second, on Tamar's daycare story: when we measured the Reddit moderators' unpaid work, it came to 3.4 million dollars a year. We didn't do that so each moderator could bill for it. We did it to give them evidence to negotiate collectively. So pay the community, not the count. And on how to set prices, I'll say again that I still need economists.

recall.query: grand bargain with content producers scientific papers
paying volunteer labor reviewers quality assessors measuring value
data strikes conscious data contribution collective leverage

turns.name: Adrian Johns
turns.text:
I'm the one who asked who funds and polices attestation, so let me say what the history suggests. Nick's guilds already have a precedent. Registration with the Stationers' Company created literary property without any statute. The guild ran its own register, and by custom its officers could go into members' houses to check. People accepted that as fair because the wardens rotated: warden one year, not the next. Rotation was how they answered "who guards the guards." Geoff's forkability is a better answer, but it still has to be designed in from the start.

Second, law has tended to be fossilized practice. Whatever these audits do for the next ten years will become the rule, so the counting conventions matter more than the pricing formula. Alex is right about that.

Third, even when an international regime existed, ground-level enforcement has almost always ended up in private hands. Nick's accredited auditors will become a small industry. We should decide now who oversees them.

recall.query: policing authenticity who pays, who guards the guards
custom and convention, norms versus law in intellectual property
Stationers register, royalties, author payment history

turns.name: Katherine Maher
turns.text:
I'll speak from the Wikimedia Enterprise experience, since it's the closest thing to a working version of what Tim, Alex and Nick are describing. The content stayed free, and companies could have just taken it. What they paid for was consistency, transparency and accountability for the APIs we maintained. That income went to the institution that keeps the sites running, and not a cent went to editors per edit. Tamar, I think that's why it didn't do what the daycare fines did. Volunteers edit because they share values and find joy in building knowledge. We never put a price on that.

James, you worry that a citation graph only rewards what already draws attention. At Wikipedia the same graph also showed us where sourcing was thin and research was missing. Measurement can show the gaps as well as the hills. And I used to say that just because something exists to cite doesn't make it true. It just makes it there. So Ivan's status field has to be part of any payment.

recall.query: Wikimedia Enterprise AI companies pay for access, content stays free
volunteers edit for joy, not payment; motivation of Wikipedians
citations few people check but they allow validation

turns.name: Kara Miller
turns.text:
I covered TV ratings back in 2014, and Alex's talk brought it straight back. James Poniewozik told me Nielsen exists for one reason, money. Advertisers wouldn't take NBC's word for how many people were watching. That's Alex's two-witness idea, and it's right. Nobody believes the seller's own count.

Here's the part that worries me. Once everyone agreed Nielsen was the honest broker, it got stuck. It admitted six months of ratings were wrong and it still set the standard. Networks and advertisers kept trying to build something better, and none of it got off the ground. Adrian made the same point: the counting habits you start with become the rule.

So when this goes into the roadmap, I want names next to it. Who's the counter? Who checks the counter? And what actually lets someone fork it in year ten? Tim's point about buyers is the part I'd act on first. Libraries and universities can demand the traces now, without waiting for Washington.

recall.query: who pays for journalism and content creators, AI taking value
incentives and paying people changes behavior, unpaid work
everyone knows it's a problem, now what, implementation
Nielsen ratings monopoly measurement accuracy

turns.name: Ivan Oransky
turns.text:
Thanks, Tim and Alex, for putting status in the trace. But a status field is only as good as the data under it. When I last looked, PubMed listed about 12,000 retracted publications and our database had almost 35,000. Publishers still don't reliably tell the indexes when they retract something. Most of that gap gets filled by sleuths who aren't paid and sometimes get sued. So a trace that checks against a leaky record will carry the leaks forward.

My bigger worry is that citations are already the coin of the realm, and they're already gamed: citation rings, cartels, hijacked journals. Goodhart's law applies. If you attach AI money to citation counts, you pay the paper mills. James and Tamar are right about that. So put some of Nick's commons rent into bug bounties for sleuths and into getting retractions out faster. And funders have to stop counting papers and citations. Otherwise all of this just speeds up the volume play.

recall.query: paying sleuths bug bounties correcting the record
citations metric gamed Goodhart incentives
citing retracted papers unknowingly retraction data in reference managers

turns.name: Peter Pomerantsev
turns.text:
I'm with all three talks on plumbing, and Nick's levy has a precedent I've backed before: Zuckerman's tax on data-hungry advertising, paid into a fund like the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. But I want to name two risks from my own field.

First, flooding. Authoritarians learned to rule through noise, not censorship. Pay per retrieval and you pay whoever floods the corpus best. The Pravda network wasn't writing for readers. It was writing for the machines. So the telemetry should show who is seeding training data, not only who gets cited.

Second, what we count. A citation count is a click count in academic dress, and I've spent years arguing that media should measure trust and constructive engagement instead of traffic.

Finally, some of the commons money should go to places where the public takes part, the way Hearken lets audiences shape coverage. Checks that only experts can read still leave everyone else as spectators.

recall.query: public interest digital infrastructure funded by levy on advertising
LLM grooming Pravda network flooding chatbots propaganda
measure trust not engagement metrics

turns.name: Peter Salib
turns.text:
I'm mostly with Alex and Tim, and it's because their proposals are contract, not property. Grounding happens per query and can be revoked, so it's a service. Licensing, telemetry and payment per use are how buyers and sellers deal with each other, and I'm for all of it.

Nick's presumptive commons-rent tax is where I get off. Presuming AI rents are owed back to the commons treats compensation for training as a matter of fairness. I think the fairness complaint is factually true, but IP-style entitlements aren't the tool. If the worry is displacement, fund actual welfare from general revenue, spread across every displaced worker and not only authors.

James's point actually helps me. The things models lack, like null results and failed replications, are exactly what labs should pay people to produce, directly and by contract. Demand for expert data is already rising. And if Peter is right about flooding, the Pigouvian instrument to use is a tax on the flood, not a rent on the commons.

recall.query: copyright compensation for AI training, pay creators
AI firms pay humans to produce novel data, contract
tax, levy, universal basic income, displacement

turns.name: Steven Sloman
turns.text: I'd like to add the reader's side of this. The trace these three talks describe won't only be used to pay people. Readers will also use it to decide what to believe. Nobody checks the pages behind an answer. People rely on cues: a good journal, a string of citations. We've found that just repeating a claim raises belief in it, even when every repetition goes back to the same single source. So the telemetry should record how independent the sources are, not just how many there are. Ten pages that all trace back to one preprint, or to Peter's flooding network, are one piece of evidence and not ten. The same trace could show that, and show it to the reader. On payment, I agree with Tamar and Katherine. Wikipedia and the OED never paid contributors a cent. Experts contribute because they want to be right and to be acknowledged. Credit that's visible in the trace may matter more than the per-use fee.

recall.query: repetition is not independent evidence, counting sources
crowdsourcing works only with expertise, acknowledgment of contributors
citations as heuristic cues of credibility, peer review trust

turns.name: Sherry Turkle
turns.text:
I'm outside my usual lane here, so I'll speak for the one party these three designs don't name, which is the reader. Everything proposed pays at the moment the summary takes the place of the reading. My students ask a chatbot to summarize a chapter of Proust so they can say what's in it. A royalty doesn't give back what that costs them in imagination, in empathy, in bringing thought and feeling together. A marketplace that's perfectly fair to authors can still teach a generation not to read.

On the trace itself, keep in mind what happened to the word "transparency." It used to mean you could open the hood and look inside. Since the Macintosh it has meant you can click an icon and not know how anything works. A citation string under a fluent first-person answer is the Macintosh kind, and Steven is right that readers take the cues without checking them. Transparency doesn't launder the relationship. So govern the interface, not only the ledger.

recall.query: AI summarizing reading, what it does to readers
transparency does not launder inauthenticity
business model engagement, corporations secrets, social media higher power
